en: And truly spill his blood.
The Zulfiqar inherited from our forefather—
If you give it, I shall gladly take it.
Against the infidel son of Sarybai,
I shall confront him and wage battle.
Seizing each other by the collar and dragging,
Struggling and hauling one another,
Striking with keen-edged swords,
Letting precious scarlet blood
Flow as we slash and crush—
Such a battle shall I wage.
If fate arrives and my days are done,
I shall surrender my dear life.
Does not every living mortal behold
The decree laid down by my Lord?
Does one not die when fate arrives?
Does a hero not die for honor?
Let me attempt the struggle;
If I do not die then, one day I shall.
For dignity and honor,
Let me join the fray.
To wage battle without restraint,
To ride out onto the field,
To brighten the hero’s brow,
To ease the ache of longing,
To issue the command,
To thrust and duel with spears,
To fight until all are spent,
To take a warrior’s life in hand,
To thrust the spear without tiring—
I learned from the transmitters,
And asked those who knew.
Its shaft is stout, its point is sharp,
With black steel fixed upon its tip;
Master of every craft,
A friend of the prophet David,
The forest smith fashioned it.
The base of the grain-dark spindlewood shaft
Was torn out with its roots.
At the fullness of summer,
Bull-necked and camel-thighed,
It destroyed men when they struggled.
The ill-omened, doom-bringing weapon
Was braced by champions.
They sheathed it in elephant hide
And thus began this great commotion.
“Summer days bring scorching heat,” they said,
“And when men grapple and fight,
It might suddenly break,” they said,
So they had it tempered in a shaded place.
“Those who take it will wage battle,” they said;
“When fierce combat and tumult arise,
The sword’s edge will strike,” they said,
So that no steel blade could cut it,
They bound it with white gold
And fashioned its many ridges.
When it came within reach
Of the holy man in your town,
When he cornered the one
Who had defied him,
He stretched and seasoned its shaft.
The patterned spear of your mighty champion—
Bölökbai and forty Kalmyks
Fashioned it with great distinction.
While they were making the spear,
A calf was slaughtered for the viewing,
And a whole forest was felled in the desert.
When the time came to temper it,
The black water boiled away to nothing.
When thrust bottomlessly at the foe,
Upon the head of whoever it struck,
Everything vanished in utter ruin.
They joined and fitted its point;
So that every one it struck
Might have his soul leave through his side,
They tempered it with tears.
Give me the splendid patterned spear,
The blue-flashing one, and let me take it;
Against the infidel son of the ogre
Let me clash and wage battle.
If true death reaches me, let me die;
Let me break the ribs
Of the enemy I truly fight.
Such is the manner of the struggle;
Let me take what I desire.
If hostile death arrives and my days are done,
Let me die without a single regret.”
Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
Had turned Jeljetpes’s head,
And, saying, “They are the hero’s inheritance,”
She asked for the patterned spear and Zulfiqar
To be given to her as gifts.
Elder Bakai, revered as a prophet,
And the noble matron Kanykei—
Saints who had witnessed much;
For the ruler’s sake, for the khan’s sake,
Your great forefather Bakai
Spread his palms and sobbed:
“From the bullet of the savage foe,
Save the lineage of the magnanimous lion;
From the infidel’s cold hands,
From the pit dug in the earth,
O Creator who grants victory in holy war,
Save them from this dog Sarybai’s snare.
Let not the fleet courser Jeljetpes
Be tethered to his post.
Almighty sovereign God,
Do not let the ogre set his eyes
Upon the warrior lion’s offspring.
Amen, my child Kuyaly.
I was the hero Bakai,
Auspicious throughout the universe,
A renowned lion.
I was the servant who opened
The value of a market held in bondage.
I was the son who unbound the hands
Of the sorrowful held captive.
I was the hero who opened the road
Through calamity tightly sealed.
I was the lion who undid the curse
Of hardship tightly entangled.
Make Sarybai the one beneath;
God, make my child the one above.
My dear child Kuyaly,
Your strength is extraordinary;
A different calamity has arisen now.
All means of defense have been exhausted;
This infidel son of the ogre,
With wrath pouring from his brow,
Has become another missile of death.
A bullet flew from the cartridge pouch,
And many bold warriors’ sons fell.
Courage fled and scattered;
The infidel son of the ogre
Appeared ready to devour them.
Only a peerless warrior
Will not flinch when shots are fired.
Unless Allah decrees it,
She does not appear destined for capture.
Fierce is the wrath of these relentless ones;
They laid flat whoever faced them.
Make him turn his back in this hour;
Keep Kuyaly, Kaiypchal’s
Champion daughter, safe!
It would bring shameful renown
If she fell to that fearsome swine.
He pledged himself to many saints,
And seven holy men showed him the way;
His father created order upon the earth
And subjugated the whole universe.
Mighty Manas, wondrous as a peri,
Please watch over
Kaiypchal’s champion daughter;
Great Manas of the mighty spirit,
Please remain her companion!
Seize the cold-faced villain
By the very hem of his robe.
Stretch the infidel who would wage war
Full-length upon the ground!
He began the campaign against Beijing,
And left it desolate.
A vast multitude, a mighty host,
He led all by himself.
He gnawed down whoever he met,
And swept away whoever crossed him.
His skill was extraordinary,
And his heroism was manifold.
Best of the noble khan’s descendants,
My dear brother, watch over her!
Do not let grievous calamity befall;
Kaiypchal, remain her companion.
His lashes were flame, his eyes embers;
No horror was absent from his wrath,
And every word he spoke was a fired bullet.
His stature differed from all men,
And his valor was manifold.
When the enemy charged with a cry,
A scarlet sword was strapped to him.
Like a cloud returning with rain,
His wrath spread across his face.
When the foe came from the flank,
He never turned aside for fear of death.
When a swarming enemy host came,
He could never stand and merely watch.
He girded his seasoned waist,
And charged through seventy ranks.
Light enough for a horse, fit for a colt,
Sleepless and vigilant upon the road—
Brave Syrgak of the young khan,
Your fortune was perfect.
For the sons of the white-capped Kyrgyz,
You were a fortress of tempered steel.
You were a young lion and hero,
The one on whom I relied.
God, set this matter right;
Valiant lion Syrgak,
Block Sarybai’s path!
God, turn the back
Of the ravenous bloodthirsty one.
The truest champion of the Oigut,
Son of Akbalta,
Whose might was known across the world.
With an unsheathed sword at his side,
Bakburchun of the forty Chinese tribes
Submitted in terror at your appearance.
Hungry lion, mighty champion,
A great upheaval cast upon the world.
Lion born of Akbaltai,
My lion, watch over us.
Offspring of the lion-hearted hero,
From this present grievous turmoil
Come and deliver us.
Agybai, son of the Argyn khan,
White-browed champion who entered the fray,
Noble-browed gray wolf among all.
You knew the tongues of sixty tribes,
Broad of jaw and fluent of tongue,
You were a hero who never faltered.
Sent ahead, you brought good fortune;
Leading the way, you were like a myriad troops,
You were one of the gray-wolf heroes.
You were the dark eye of the gray wolves,
You were nobility itself.
Watch over us,
Protect my child.
Each of you was a living hero:
Yrchy-uul of the Katagan,
And valiant Shuutu in his felt-cap;
Tölöchü, son of Tölöman,
The darling of your four households;
Baichoro, son of Baabedin,
Watch over us.
All of the forty companions,
Their elder, led by Kyrgyl,
Remain his comrades!”
So mighty Bakai spoke,
Shouting out his blessing,
Stirring the whole world,
And calling upon the spirits
Of the companions gone to the next world.
His face grew pale and drawn,
And tears streamed from both eyes,
Pouring down upon his breast.
“Wretched, meaningless world!” he said,
And sought refuge in the warrior maiden,
Slung his prayer-pouch around his neck,
And pleaded with the Creator:
“May the Maker grant us favor!”
In his old age, Bakai’s
Heart burned and grieved.
A man’s deafness is a bitter thing,
Leaving him no better than the black earth.
It was wise of Almighty God, who created us,
Not to let life linger overlong,
But to take it away.
The burden of years is a snare,
